stories.headline: OpenSSH “sshole” flaw lets attackers bypass passwordless accounts on Alpine Linux
stories.in_brief: A decade‑old vulnerability in OpenSSH when built with the musl C library lets attackers log in to password‑disabled Alpine Linux accounts by sending an oversized password. The flaw, dubbed *sshole, has been patched in OpenSSH 10.6p2 and Alpine packages, but attacks were observed within hours of disclosure.
stories.so_what: The vulnerability, tracked as CVE‑2026‑123158, affects any Linux system that uses musl (including Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto) with OpenSSH compiled without PAM and password authentication enabled. Exploitation requires only network access, an account name and a password longer than 256 bytes, allowing a single‑connection login without retries. While root accounts remain protected by default settings, compromised passwordless accounts with doas or sudo rights can be leveraged for full system takeover. The rapid exploitation reported by threat‑intel firm Previdian underscores the need for immediate remediation. Administrators should upgrade OpenSSH to version 10.6p2 or later and ensure Alpine packages are updated, while users should verify that password authentication is disabled or that PAM is enabled to block the attack vector.
stories.what_to_do: 1. Upgrade OpenSSH to version 10.6p2 or newer (apk upgrade openssh). 2. Disable PasswordAuthentication in sshd_config or enable PAM. 3. Verify no accounts have ‘*’ in /etc/shadow unless intentionally password‑less.

claims.quote: OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16.

claims.claim: The vulnerability was exploited in the wild within nine hours of its public disclosure.
claims.quote: Our first observed attempt arrived less than nine hours after CVE publication, and we’ve confirmed successful root access on a Previdian honeypot running real Alpine Linux and OpenSSH.

stories.headline: White House Network Used as Residential Proxy Exit Points
stories.in_brief: Security researchers found that devices on the White House network acted as residential proxy exit nodes, allowing external users to route traffic through White House IP addresses. The activity was observed mainly in evenings and involved multiple proxy services.
stories.so_what: The discovery shows that even highly secured government networks can be inadvertently leveraged to provide public proxy services, potentially exposing internal traffic to external observers and facilitating malicious activities such as account takeover or content scraping. The proxy nodes were traced to six IP addresses within the Executive Office’s AS2650 range and were active on 26 of 30 days between October 5 and November 3, exiting 236 times. Twenty‑eight different residential proxy providers were able to use these exits, with most traffic occurring between 5 p.m. and midnight Eastern Time, suggesting a user’s device infected with a proxy SDK was responsible. Organizations should audit devices for unauthorized SDKs, especially on Windows 10/11 systems, and consider stricter network segmentation to prevent similar misuse.
stories.what_to_do: 1. Verify that all Windows 10 and Windows 11 machines are free of unauthorized proxy SDKs (e.g., InfaticaSDK, Rave.io). 2. Apply the latest security patches and enable endpoint protection that can detect proxy‑related malware. 3. Review network segmentation and restrict outbound traffic from sensitive IP ranges to only approved destinations.

stories.headline: Hubble images reveal ancient globular cluster M30’s distance and possible extragalactic origin
stories.in_brief: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope captured new data on globular cluster Messier 30, located about 27,500 light‑years away. The findings highlight the cluster’s extreme age and its retrograde orbit, suggesting it may have been captured by the Milky Way.
stories.so_what: Messier 30 (M30) is a globular cluster situated roughly 27,500 light‑years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus. Globular clusters are among the oldest stellar systems, with ages estimated between 11.5 and 13.5 billion years, making them valuable time capsules for studying early galactic chemistry. Recent Hubble observations, using the Wide Field Camera 3, have confirmed that M30, like many other clusters, orbits opposite to the Milky Way’s rotation, a pattern that implies it may not have formed within our galaxy but was instead captured long ago. Understanding such captured clusters helps astronomers refine models of the Milky Way’s growth through mergers and accretion. Future observations will aim to map the motions of additional clusters to assess how common extragalactic capture has been in the galaxy’s history.

Reissuance beginning in 2031 adds a new source of supply without exceeding the 21 million coin cap, preserving scarcity while funding security.
